text.p: These are some of the main stories in Sofia newspapers on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
-- Thousands of Bulgarians gathered in central Sofia on Tuesday evening to protest against the economic and social policies of the Socialist government and to demand its resignation.

-- The main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) will not take part in any coalition government with the Socialists after the presidential elections due on October 27, an UDF deputy said, denying local media reports. He said the opposition would seek early parliamentary elections to end the Socialists' majority.
-- The prices of goods monitored by the cabinet rose by 13 percent in the first half of October, National Statistics Institute said.
-- The debt of Bulgaria's largest oil refinery Neftochim exceeds 12 billion levs, which is almost as much as its assets of 13.5 billion levs, the refinery's trade union said.

-- The Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) will not cut its main interest rate of 300 percent at this stage, BNB governor Lyubomir Filipov told the parliamentary group of the ruling socialists. Socialist deputies asked the central bank to cut its record high main interest rate of 300 percent as it is affecting Bulgaria's production.

-- Bulgaria will have to import 1.5 million tonnes of grain for human and animal consumption to meet the country's 1996 - 1997 grain balance of five million tonnes, deputy agriculture minister Dimo Uzunov said.
-- Bulgaria's exports to the United Kingdom rose by 16 percent in the first seven months of 1996, compared to the same period in the previous year, visiting British businessmen said.
-- The consumption of meat in Bulgaria has fallen by one third compared to the last year, the agriculture ministry said.
-- Bulgaria will have to import 15,000 tonnes of beans, 31,000 tonnes of rice and 73,000 tonnes of potatoes to secure the country's food balance, the agriculture ministry said.
-- Some five billion levs from the state budget are blocked in the nine banks placed under special supervision by the central bank on September 23, the newspaper said, without quoting sources.
-- Some of the nine banks under special supervision could be stabilised rather than closed, BNB governor Lyubomir Filipov said.
-- The killer of former prime minister and socialist deputy Andrei Lukanov, who was shot dead on October 2, is most likely a man of Chechen origin, the newspaper said. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
